title: Foreword
text:
FIRST EDITION 2026 | MESSAGE FROM THE PRESIDENT
Foreword

The maritime profession is international by its very nature. A ship may be built in one country, owned in another,
managed from another, and operated by seafarers of many different nationalities. In such an environment,
English is more than an academic subject. It is a professional tool — and, at sea, clear communication is an
essential part of safe and effective operations.
Throughout my years at sea and later in ship management and maritime education, I have seen that technical
knowledge alone does not make a competent maritime professional. A seafarer must also be able to understand
instructions, ask the right questions, communicate clearly, report facts accurately, and speak with confidence
when circumstances become difficult.
This is why I am particularly pleased to introduce Maritime English 3.17 Plus, prepared by Dr. Wayne Vincent
Tolomia, Head of Foreign Languages, Academic Affairs, Asian Maritime Technological College (AMCOL). This
course book has been developed specifically for both deck and engine cadets, integrating language learning with
the professional situations they are likely to encounter throughout their careers.
What I especially appreciate about this book is its practical approach. The ten units take learners progressively
from joining a ship and becoming familiar with the shipboard environment to watchkeeping, position and weather
reporting, VHF communication, distress and safety communication, mooring and anchoring, cargo operations,
machinery and maintenance, and finally incident reporting and handover.
The book does not treat English as vocabulary and grammar in isolation. Students are repeatedly required to
read, listen, speak, write, clarify, confirm, record and report. Its learning sequence moves from vocabulary and
models to documents, reading, grammar, speaking, practical language tasks, worksheets and assessment. This
reflects an important principle of maritime education: competence is demonstrated not by what we know, but by
what we can apply correctly when it matters.
I also value the emphasis placed throughout this book on accuracy and professional judgement. Students are
encouraged to distinguish facts from assumptions, preserve figures and units correctly, request clarification when
information is uncertain, and avoid inventing missing information. These habits extend far beyond language
learning. They are fundamental behaviours of competent officers and responsible maritime professionals.
At AMCOL, our responsibility is not simply to prepare students to pass examinations. Our greater responsibility is
to prepare them for the reality of  life and work at sea — and ultimately to develop professionals who can
contribute confidently and responsibly to the global maritime industry.
I therefore sincerely commend Dr. Wayne Vincent Tolomia for the considerable effort, professional dedication
and educational thought invested in preparing this first edition. Developing a course book of this scope requires
not only knowledge of English teaching, but also a genuine commitment to understanding the communication
needs of future seafarers. This work is a valuable contribution to the continuing development of Maritime English
education at AMCOL.
To every cadet who uses this book, I offer one message:
  Do not study Maritime English simply to pass an examination. Learn it so that one day, when you
   stand on a bridge, work in an engine room, communicate with a multinational team, or face a difficult
   situation at sea, you can understand clearly, think professionally, and communicate with confidence.
May this book become not only a classroom resource, but also the beginning of a lifelong habit of clear, accurate
and professional maritime communication.

Dr. Chalermvut Thansuvan
President
Asian Maritime Technological College (AMCOL)
Former Master Mariner
Thailand

title: Preface
text:
FIRST EDITION 2026 | READING, PRACTICE AND ASSESSMENT

Preface

Maritime English 3.17 Plus is a course book and workbook for deck and engine cadets. It develops the
English needed to understand shipboard information, ask useful questions, exchange clear messages
and produce factual records. The ten units connect language study with situations from joining a ship
to reporting an incident and handing over unfinished work.

Each of the ten units includes a dedicated reading article. Dialogues, shipboard documents and
articles serve different purposes: listen to an exchange, locate information in a record, and follow ideas
across paragraphs. Each article has ten comprehension and application questions. Visual resources
provide the plans, cards and forms needed for the linked tasks.

Read, practise, produce and review

Begin with the vocabulary and study the model. Read a text once for its main purpose, then again for
details and evidence. Practise the grammar before writing or speaking independently. Use the supplied
data accurately, keep uncertain information labelled, and revise your work after feedback. A request for
clarification is part of successful communication, not a failure.

For deck and engine learners

Both departments need accurate names, figures, locations, time references and status reports. Some
tasks are department-specific, but mixed pairs can explain their information to each other. Do not claim
an officer's qualification when practising a cadet introduction: state your actual training role and the
documents relevant to it.

Using this book responsibly

The situations and numerical data are teaching examples. Follow actual shipboard procedures,
authorised personnel and applicable requirements in practice. The book supports language learning; it
does not authorise navigation, maintenance, firefighting, cargo handling or radio operation. Distress
practice is conducted only in a closed classroom simulation.

The final assessment contains 150 short-response items and four writing/speaking tasks, totalling 240
marks. A separate teacher supplement provides reading keys, visual guidance, listening scripts, final
assessment answers and rubrics. Teaching and examination times are starting points for local piloting,
not validated limits.

Dr. Wayne Vincent Tolomia

Asian Maritime Technological College | Chonburi, Thailand

STCW Competency Coverage

IMO Model Course 3.17 organises teaching into General Maritime English and Specialized Maritime English [S1].
The lists below identify the STCW English and communication elements practised in this publication. Headings
are shortened teaching labels; coverage statements are editorial mappings of the printed activities, not
quotations from the Code.

This course book combines a common deck-and-engine language foundation with selected occupational applications. Dialogues,
documents, articles, visual tasks and assessments provide different kinds of language evidence.

  A-II/1          Maritime English and SMCP for deck officers

  PRIMARY | SELECTED LANGUAGE ELEMENTS

  Understand and exchange shipboard information; describe positions and weather; use relevant standard
  phrases; interpret notices and records; write clear operational messages.

  Evidence in this book: Units 1-10, especially Units 3-8 and 10; B/B2/B3 reading strands; speaking and practical tasks. [S2]

   A-III/1          English for engineering duties

  PRIMARY | SELECTED LANGUAGE ELEMENTS

  Describe machinery and its location, understand routine engineering information, report faults and read the
  supplied procedures and maintenance records in English.

  Evidence in this book: Units 1-3, 6, 9 and 10; engine handover, work-order and machinery-status tasks. Coverage is
   limited to the technical texts supplied in the book. [S2]

  A-IV/2          English in maritime radio message handling

   LIMITED | LANGUAGE COMPONENT ONLY

  Practise identification, clarification, confirmation and recording of radio information; construct and interpret
  the supplied distress, urgency and safety exchanges.

  Evidence in this book: Units 5-6 and their message forms. Classroom transmissions do not establish GMDSS equipment
  competence or authority to operate a live radio. [S2]

  A-VI/1-4        Effective communication on board

  PRIMARY | COMMUNICATION ELEMENT

  Ask about duties and locations, understand safety-related instructions, pass accurate information and
  request repetition when a message is unclear.

  Evidence in this book: Units 1-3, 6-7, 9-10; partner tasks, feedback and handovers. The remaining Personal Safety and
   Social Responsibilities requirements are not claimed. [S3]

How to read this map. Primary identifies a direct language aim; contextual identifies communication within a wider operational competency;
limited identifies only a particular transferable element. None means that the whole STCW competency is taught, assessed or certified by
this book.

PREFACE CONTINUED | CONTEXTUAL COVERAGE

Operational Communication Links

These links concern the English used within a wider competency. The named activity is evidence of language
practice, not evidence that the learner can independently perform the full operation. [S2]

  A-II/1          Navigational watch and bridge-team communication

  Communicate a present situation, relevant figures, standing instructions and unfinished work; record
  information so that another watch can understand it.

  Evidence in this book: Units 3-5, 7 and 10: handover, weather and passage messages, VHF log and incident records. This is
  not a practical navigation qualification. [S2]

   A-III/1          Engineering watch and internal communication

  Exchange engine-room status, report readings and defects, and transfer outstanding actions. The
  internal-communication link concerns clear messages and records, not hardware operation.

  Evidence in this book: Units 3, 6, 9 and 10: engine log, fault report, maintenance work order and handover. [S2]

  A-II/4           English helm orders

  Give and repeat standard wheel orders and preserve the stated figure. This supports the English component
  of the rating competency; actual steering performance must be trained and assessed separately.

  Evidence in this book: Unit 3: standard-order practice and the order/repeat-back drill. [S2]

  A-II/1         Communication during cargo handling

   Identify cargo information and a reported discrepancy, communicate a stopped or pending operation, and
  prepare a factual written record.

  Evidence in this book: Unit 8: cargo dialogue, document, reading article and visual tasks. A completed language exercise is
  not a stowage, segregation or cargo-safety approval. [S2]

text:
A REPEATABLE LEARNING SEQUENCE

How to Use a Unit

 Section               What you do

 A Vocabulary            Say the terms, check meanings and use them in a short example.

 B Dialogue / listening        Identify the speakers, the situation, important figures and the purpose of each
                         message.

 B2 Written document      Read a form, log, report or notice; connect information with the exchange.

                              short application.

 C / C2 Grammar           Study form and meaning, complete controlled practice, then build and produce
                            your own sentences.

 D Speaking             Use role information, ask for clarification and confirm critical details.

                           handover.

 V Visual resources       Read and complete the diagrams, forms and role cards linked to D/E.

 F Worksheet             Review the unit independently and check your progress.

Make your work easy to check

Keep figures beside their units. Identify the source of a statement. Distinguish a plan from a completed
action. Use “not stated” or “not confirmed” rather than inventing a missing fact. In a report, retain an
approximate time as approximate. After feedback, make the correction and use the improved version in the
next task.

title: First Hour on Board
text:
UNIT 1 | B READING AND LISTENING

First Hour on Board

  The situation
 MV Andaman Trader is alongside in Laem Chabang. A new Third Officer and Fourth Engineer report to the
  ship's office. All times in this exchange are local time.

CHIEF OFFICER Good afternoon. Welcome on board. Please give your names and ranks.

THIRD OFFICER Somchai Prasert, joining as Third Officer. My certificate of competency and passport are
here.

FOURTH ENGINEER Nuttapong Wong, joining as Fourth Engineer.

CHIEF OFFICER Thank you. You sign on today, 4 March. Mr Prasert, you work to me. Mr Wong, you report to
the Second Engineer.

THIRD OFFICER Which watch will I keep?

CHIEF OFFICER The 0800-1200 and 2000-2400 watches. You relieve the Second Officer at 0800 tomorrow.

FOURTH ENGINEER Is the engine room manned at night?

CHIEF OFFICER It is periodically unattended at night, with a duty engineer on call. The Second Engineer will
explain the arrangements and confirm your assignment after familiarisation.

THIRD OFFICER Where is my muster station?

CHIEF OFFICER Lifeboat station number two, port side, boat deck. Your personal lifejacket and immersion suit
are in your cabin. Check the muster list with your trainer.

FOURTH ENGINEER When is safety familiarisation?

CHIEF OFFICER Today, before you start duties. The bosun leads the deck tour at 1600; the Second Engineer
takes you through the machinery spaces. Ask about anything unclear and record what has been completed.

THIRD OFFICER Is there a handover from the officer I am relieving?

CHIEF OFFICER Yes. The outgoing Third Officer remains aboard until 1800. Meet in the office at 1700, discuss
his notes and both sign the handover record.

Original classroom dialogue adapted from the supplied manuscript. Operational data are fictional; this is not a complete operating procedure.

Familiarisation principle: S3. The times and reporting arrangements describe this fictional ship only.

title: Joining a New Ship: More Than Paperwork
text:
UNIT 1 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

Joining a New Ship: More Than Paperwork

  Before you read
  Look at the crew chart in Visual Resource 1. Which officer would a deck cadet normally ask for help?

Reading focus: Find responsibilities and put joining activities in order.

A A new ship has familiar job titles but unfamiliar spaces, equipment and people. Joining is therefore
more than handing over a passport. A new crew member needs to know who gives instructions, where to
go in an emergency and how to ask for help. The first conversation starts this process; it does not finish it.

B On MV Blue Horizon, deck cadet Mali reports to the Chief Officer. Engine cadet Arun reports to the
Second Engineer for daily training. At 1400 both cadets check their joining details in the ship's office.
They present the training documents required for their roles. Neither cadet claims to hold an officer's
certificate of competency.

C Before they are assigned shipboard duties, they receive the required safety information and
familiarisation. At 1430 an authorised crew member shows them their muster station and escape routes.
Mali then explains the route back without help. Arun cannot identify the alternative exit, so he asks to see
it again instead of signing that part as understood.

D At 1530 the trainer checks their understanding and records what they have completed. Any unfinished
training is identified before duties are assigned. A signature records the training, but it cannot replace
understanding. Both cadets keep a short list of questions for their next meeting with their supervisors.

Word support

assigned: given a particular duty   |  demonstrate: show how to do something   |  record: a written account

title: Present simple for roles and routines
text:
UNIT 1 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Present simple for roles and routines

Use the present simple for a role, a regular duty or a fixed schedule. Use be for identity and state; use other
verbs for actions. Choose the form from the subject.

 Meaning             Form                      Example

 Role / state           am / is / are                  The Chief Engineer is responsible for machinery.

 Routine action             subject + verb; he/she/it + -s     The bosun checks the deck every morning.

 Negative action          do not / does not + base verb     The cadet does not sign as an officer.

 Negative with be       am / is / are + not              The engineer is not on watch now.

 Question with action     Do / Does + subject + base      Does the officer keep the 0800 watch?
                          verb?

 Question with be       Am / Is / Are + subject ...?           Is the Chief Officer on board?

Build the sentence

The Third Officer + keeps + the 0800-1200 watch. Change only the verb when the subject changes: The
officers keep the watch. After does, return to the base form: Does she keep ...?

Spelling and pronunciation

Most verbs add -s: runs, signs. Add -es after endings such as -sh, -ch, -ss, -x and -o: watches, passes, goes.
Consonant + y changes to -ies: carries. Have becomes has. Practise the endings in checks, runs and
watches.

Put frequency words in a clear place

Usually, always and normally generally come before an action verb but after be: The engineer usually checks
the alarms. The engineer is usually available. A schedule in this book describes its fictional vessel, not every
ship.

Examples are for language learning. Sources: S1; see editorial notes.

text:

Examples and controlled practice

  Check a common error

B  READING AND LISTENING

  THE SITUATION

  The bosun is taking the new Third Officer around the deck while the Second Engineer takes the new Fourth Engineer below.
   Both tours meet in the alleyway.

Familiarisation Tour                                                                     Recording script - approx. 3 minutes

  BOSUN
  We start forward. This is the forecastle. The windlass and both anchors are here, and the forward mooring station is just behind
   you.

  THIRD OFFICER
  And the cargo holds? How many does she have?

  BOSUN
   Four. Hold number one is directly aft of the forecastle. Walk aft along the starboard side and you pass all four hatch covers.

  THIRD OFFICER
  Where is the fire station on this deck?

  BOSUN
  There are two. One at the forward end of the alleyway, one aft. Hoses, extinguishers and two sets of fire gear at each.

  SECOND ENGINEER
  Down here we are two decks below the main deck. This is the engine control room. Everything is monitored from this panel.

  FOURTH ENGINEER
   Is the main engine forward or aft of us?

  SECOND ENGINEER
   Forward. Go through that watertight door and down one more level and you are on the engine room floor plates. The workshop is
    aft, behind you, and the purifier room is above it.

  FOURTH ENGINEER
  Where do I sound the bilges?

  SECOND ENGINEER
  The sounding pipes are on the starboard side at floor plate level. You record the figures in the engine logbook every watch.

  FOURTH ENGINEER
  And the escape route from down here, sir?

  SECOND ENGINEER
  Good. There are two. The main stairway the way we came, and an emergency escape trunk on the port side that comes out on the boat
   deck. Walk it during familiarisation and learn the marked route. Do not rely on memory alone.

  BOSUN
  Same rule on deck. Your muster station is boat deck, port side, at lifeboat number two. Walk the approved route from your cabin and
   identify the signs and landmarks.

Finding Your Way - and Your Way Out

  Before you read
 Name one word that describes a deck level and one word that describes a side of a ship.

Reading focus: Combine location words with a simple vessel plan.

A A location is clearer when it includes a named space and a deck level. Left and right can change when
a person turns around. Port and starboard describe the vessel's sides when facing forward. A cadet can
therefore use them even when the listener is facing a different direction.

B On the training vessel in Visual Resource 2, the bridge is on Deck 5. The radio room is next to it.
Cabins are on Deck 3, and the galley and messroom are on Deck 2. The engine control room is on Deck
1. The workshop is aft of the engine control room on the same deck.

C A main stairway connects Decks 1 to 5. From the Deck 3 cabin alleyway, the normal route to the
muster station goes up one deck to the port side of Deck 4. A separate escape trunk connects Deck 1
directly to Deck 4. It provides an alternative way out from the machinery area.

D During familiarisation, the trainer shows both routes and asks cadets to explain them. A box in an
alleyway is reported, not ignored. If a route is obstructed during an emergency, crew follow the ship's
emergency instructions and use a safe available alternative. The classroom plan helps students practise
language; it is not the arrangement of every vessel.

title: Prepositions of place; there is / there are
text:
UNIT 2 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Prepositions of place; there is / there are

Use there is or there are to introduce something in a location. Use a preposition to place it relative to another
named object. Do not expect the listener to guess which deck or side you mean.

 Meaning             Form                      Example

 One item                There is + singular noun         There is a fire station beside the door.

 Two or more             There are + plural noun          There are two escape routes.

 Negative                There is not / There are not       There are not any boxes in the alleyway.

 Question                      Is there / Are there ...?               Is there an escape trunk on this deck?

 Higher / lower           above / below                 The bridge is above the cabins.

 Ship direction             forward of / aft of; on the port     The workshop is aft of the control room.
                             side

Choose the reference point

The radio room is next to the bridge. The object being located is the radio room; the reference point is the
bridge. Reversing a relation can change the meaning: A is above B means B is below A.

On, in and at

Use on with a deck or side: on Deck 4, on the port side. Common shipboard phrases include on the bridge, in
the engine room and at the muster station. Learn the complete phrase.

Introduce, then describe

There is an extinguisher here. It is beside the door. There introduces its existence; it refers to the extinguisher
already mentioned. Use ship directions when they remove ambiguity; ordinary next to and behind remain
useful with a clear reference.

Examples are for language learning. Sources: S1; see editorial notes.

title: Why a Handover Needs More Than “Everything Is
text:
UNIT 3 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

Why a Handover Needs More Than “Everything Is
Fine”

  Before you read
  What information would you need before taking over a task from another person?

Reading focus: Separate normal arrangements, current changes and outstanding work.

A At a watch handover, the next officer needs a clear picture of the vessel now. Everything is fine does
not explain which equipment is working, which task is unfinished or when another check is due. A useful
handover makes changes easy to notice.

B On MV Blue Horizon, the bridge handover begins at 0800. The outgoing officer reports that visibility is
decreasing in rain. The next weather update is due at 0830. The incoming officer records both the
present condition and the time of the next update. The officer also checks the applicable standing orders.

C In the engine control room, the engineers discuss a different change. No. 2 fresh-water pump is out of
service, and No. 1 pump is in use. The fault was recorded at 0645. The Second Engineer has arranged
an inspection for 1000, but the cause has not yet been confirmed. A planned inspection is not a
completed repair.

D The receiving officer asks questions about anything unclear. Important figures are checked, and
unfinished work is recorded with a responsible person and a time. On this vessel, the handover record
separates normal arrangements, current changes and outstanding work. This helps the next watch see
what needs attention without treating an assumption as a fact.

Word support

outstanding: not yet completed   |  current: true at the present time   |  confirmed: checked and established

notes.

title: Present continuous and present simple
text:
UNIT 3 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Present continuous and present simple

The present continuous describes an action happening now or a temporary situation. The present simple
describes a regular duty or standing fact. Both can appear in a handover, but they give different information.

 Meaning             Form                      Example

  Action now           am / is / are + verb-ing          The main engine is running at 72 RPM.

 Temporary situation     am / is / are + verb-ing        We are steering by hand during this approach.

 Routine                   present simple                The duty engineer makes rounds every two
                                                              hours.

 Negative now         am / is / are + not + verb-ing      No. 1 generator is not running.

 Question now        Am / Is / Are + subject +             Is the purifier running normally?
                            verb-ing?

 State in this meaning       usually present simple                     I understand the instruction.

Build and check the verb phrase

The officer + is + monitoring + the target. The -ing word needs am, is or are. In a question, put the helper first:
Is the officer monitoring the target?

Spelling

Usually add -ing: check -> checking. Drop a silent final e: make -> making. Some short verbs double the last
consonant: run -> running, stop -> stopping. Learn these common forms as a set.

Use the situation, not just a signal word

Now and currently often suggest the continuous. Every watch often suggests a routine, but temporary
repeated actions can also use the continuous. State verbs such as know, understand and need normally use
the simple form in these examples.

text:
UNIT 4 | B READING AND LISTENING

The Noon Position and the Forecast

  The situation
  Noon on 4 March. These classroom calculations assume constant speed along the remaining route and no
  additional delay. Real passage decisions require the full navigational assessment.

MASTER What is our noon position?

SECOND OFFICER Latitude one one degrees four zero minutes North; longitude one zero zero degrees one
two minutes East. Distance run in the last twenty-four hours is three zero two decimal five nautical miles.

MASTER What are the present heading and speed?

SECOND OFFICER Heading zero eight five degrees gyro; speed twelve decimal four knots. We have two two
nine decimal four nautical miles to run along the remaining route.

MASTER What is the forecast for tonight?

SECOND OFFICER Wind south-west force five now, increasing to force seven after midnight. The sea is
moderate, becoming rough, with a north-easterly swell of about two metres.

MASTER And visibility?

SECOND OFFICER Six nautical miles now. The forecast gives two nautical miles or less in rain squalls
between 0200 and 0600.

MASTER We are going to secure movable objects and check the hatch cleats before 1700. Inform the Chief
Officer and the engine room. What is the ETA?

SECOND OFFICER At twelve decimal four knots, 0630 tomorrow. If we maintain that speed until midnight and
then reduce to eight knots, the calculated ETA is about 1005 tomorrow.

MASTER Send the later planning estimate to the agent and state the speed assumption. I will review the
course and speed at 0400 if the motion becomes bad.

SECOND OFFICER Understood. I will record the forecast, the planned actions and the ETA assumptions
separately.

text:
UNIT 4 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

From Forecast to Passage Decision

  Before you read
  Which is a measurement: “visibility is six miles” or “visibility may decrease tonight”?

Reading focus: Distinguish observation, forecast and planned response.

A A weather report and a forecast answer different questions. A report describes conditions observed at
a stated time. A forecast describes what is expected during a future period in an area. When an officer
combines them, the record should make the difference clear.

B At 1200 LT on 18 September, MV Cedar Bay has 96 nautical miles remaining to its pilot station. Its
planning speed is 12 knots. The noon observation gives south-westerly wind force 4 and visibility of six
nautical miles. If that speed is maintained along the remaining route without delay, the passage takes
eight hours and the ETA is 2000 LT the same day.

C The latest forecast expects visibility to decrease to two nautical miles in rain between 1600 and 2000.
This is not a measurement already made at noon. The Master plans to review conditions at 1530 and has
ordered a deck inspection by 1500. The engine room has been asked to report machinery readiness by
1545. Both departments need the same times.

D At 1530 the vessel still has 54 nautical miles to run. For this classroom calculation, the Master sets a
new planning speed of nine knots for all of that distance. Six hours remain, so the revised ETA is 2130
LT. The officer tells the pilot station the new ETA and records its assumptions. A forecast, a speed
calculation and a booking are related, but they are not the same kind of information.

in planning but not guaranteed

title: Talking about the future
text:
UNIT 4 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Talking about the future

Will, going to, the present continuous and the present simple can all refer to the future. Their meanings
overlap. A form may emphasise a decision, plan, prediction, arrangement or timetable; it does not by itself
prove that a plan is fixed or changeable.

 Emphasis            Form                      Example

 Decision / offer now          will + base verb                                I will call the pilot station now.

  Prediction / expectation      will + base verb                        Visibility will improve, according to the forecast.

  Existing intention           am/is/are going to + base verb   We are going to check the deck, as agreed.

  Prediction from evidence   am/is/are going to + base verb    Those dark clouds suggest it is going to rain.

 Arranged future event      am/is/are + verb-ing + future     The inspector is arriving at 1000 tomorrow.
                            time

 Timetable                 present simple                The briefing starts at 0900 tomorrow.

Check the whole message

The pilot will board at 0630 can be grammatical even when boarding is arranged. The pilot is boarding at 0630
emphasises the arrangement. Add clear words such as confirmed, planned or subject to weather when the
status matters.

Form the negative and question

Will not + base verb: We will not enter yet. Will + subject + base verb: Will visibility improve? For going to: Are
we going to secure the deck? Do not put -s or -ing directly after will.

Practice instructions specify the target

When an exercise asks for present continuous, use that form to show the arrangement. This is a
transformation task, not a claim that another grammatical future form is an error. A forecast remains a
prediction, not a completed observation.

title: When a Radio Message Is Not Clear
text:
UNIT 5 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

When a Radio Message Is Not Clear

  Before you read
  What could go wrong if a listener guesses a draft or arrival time?

Reading focus: Recognise a communication problem and follow its repair.

A A clear voice does not always produce a clear message. Background noise can hide a digit, and a
familiar word can lead a listener to guess the rest. A useful response identifies the part that was not
understood. Guessing a vessel's draft or arrival time does not solve the problem.

B In a classroom exchange, MV Sea Lantern calls Harbour Control. The vessel reports a draft of 8.4
metres. A noise hides the decimal part, so the shore operator asks for the draft again. The officer repeats
8.4 metres slowly. Harbour Control reads the figure back, and the officer confirms it. Only then does the
operator enter the figure in the record.

C Later, the officer gives an ETA of 1740 LT, then notices an error in the notes. The officer says
CORRECTION and gives 1750 LT. Harbour Control confirms the corrected time. The current ETA field
shows 1750; the communication log also records that the earlier figure was corrected. The original error
must not silently become the current value.

D Message markers can help show whether a message gives information, asks a question or requests
action. They are not compulsory before every sentence. Standard procedure words help manage the
exchange: OVER expects a reply, while OUT closes the exchange. A short request such as Say again,
please is acceptable. The aim is a shared understanding of the message, not unnecessary words or an
artificial ban on politeness.

Word support

distorted: changed so it is hard to hear clearly   |  clarification: extra information that makes meaning clear   |
acknowledgement: a response showing receipt

title: Imperatives and requests
text:
UNIT 5 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Imperatives and requests

An imperative gives a direct instruction. A question with may or could can make a request. On the radio, the
function, operational context and speaker's responsibility matter as well as grammar. Keep the message
short without changing its intended meaning.

 Function             Form                      Example

  Instruction              base verb + object               Switch to VHF Channel one two.

  Prohibition            Do not + base verb           Do not enter the fairway.

 Request for permission   May I + base verb ...?          May I enter the fairway?

 Statement of need               I require / I request ...                      I require a pilot.

 Advice               ADVICE + recommendation      ADVICE. Advise you contact Port Control.

 Warning             WARNING + stated danger      WARNING. A vessel is approaching the
                                                              entrance.

Message markers help identify purpose

The eight SMCP markers are INSTRUCTION, ADVICE, WARNING, INFORMATION, QUESTION, ANSWER,
REQUEST and INTENTION. The SMCP says they may be used. Do not add one mechanically to every
transmission.

Polite does not mean long

Say again, please is an accepted communication-repair form. Please is not banned. Avoid long, indirect
wording that makes an instruction difficult to recognise. A request does not create authority or permission by
itself.

Confirm what was understood

For important information, confirm the exact figure or ask for it again. An acknowledgement, a read-back and a
report of completed action are different. OVER invites a reply; OUT ends an exchange when no reply is
expected.

Examples are for language learning. Sources: S1; S2.

Fire in the Engine Room

  The situation
  At 0212 LT a fire is reported on the fuel-oil purifier. This is a closed classroom communication case. The
  transcript does not authorise entry, CO2 release or any real firefighting action.

SECOND ENGINEER Bridge, engine control room. Fire at the fuel-oil purifier. The purifier has been stopped and
the fuel supply isolated under the emergency procedure. The engine-room team has withdrawn.

MASTER Sound the general alarm. Confirm the headcount and report to the emergency command team.

SECOND ENGINEER At 0216, all twenty-one persons are accounted for. No injury has been reported. The fire
is not under control.

MASTER MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is motor vessel ANDAMAN TRADER, ANDAMAN TRADER,
ANDAMAN TRADER. Call sign Hotel Sierra Alfa X-ray Four. MAYDAY. ANDAMAN TRADER. My position is one
one degrees four zero minutes North, one zero zero degrees one two minutes East. I am on fire in the engine
room. The fire is not under control. I require immediate assistance. I have two one persons on board. Over.

COAST RADIO ANDAMAN TRADER, this is Coast Radio. Received MAYDAY. Say again your position. Over.

MASTER My position is one one degrees four zero minutes North, one zero zero degrees one two minutes East.
Over.

COAST RADIO Position received. Assistance is being arranged. Are you abandoning ship? Over.

title: Choosing the Right Emergency Message
text:
UNIT 6 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

Choosing the Right Emergency Message

  Before you read
  Does the name of an equipment fault alone tell you how serious a situation is?

Reading focus: Read the stated danger before choosing a signal.

A The signal at the start of a message tells listeners its priority. MAYDAY concerns grave and imminent
danger requiring immediate assistance. PAN-PAN introduces an urgent safety message below that level.
SECURITE introduces safety information, such as a navigational or weather warning. The facts of the
situation matter more than a single word such as failure.

B Consider three invented training cards. Card A describes uncontrolled flooding. The vessel is losing
stability and the Master requires immediate assistance. There are 18 persons on board. The card gives
the position as 12 degrees 20 minutes North, 100 degrees 10 minutes East at 0900 UTC. The transmitter
must give these facts clearly rather than spending the first turn explaining a possible cause.

C Card B describes a propulsion failure in open water, clear of traffic and danger. The Master states that
the vessel and people are not in grave or imminent danger, but urgent assistance is needed. Card C
describes an unlit drifting object near a shipping route. The reporting vessel is safe and is warning others.
These facts lead to different signals even though all three cards concern safety.

D The receiver records the identity, position, problem and requested assistance relevant to the message.
Missing or unclear information is requested, not invented. If the danger changes, the responsible officer
reassesses the communication priority. In class, students use disconnected equipment or a closed
simulator. No practice distress message is transmitted on an operational radio channel. The exercise
teaches language, not a complete emergency or GMDSS procedure.

Word support

imminent: about to happen   |  urgency: a need for prompt attention   |  available: ready or able to be used

title: Imperatives and passive emergency reports
text:
UNIT 6 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Imperatives and passive emergency reports

Use a clear imperative for an instruction and an accurate statement for a report. The passive puts the action
or affected object first. It does not remove the need to identify a responsible person when that information
matters.

 Meaning             Form                      Example

  Instruction              base verb                    Sound the general alarm.

  Prohibition            Do not + base verb           Do not enter the space.

 Present status               is/are + past participle                All personnel are accounted for.

 Completed past action     was/were + past participle       The alarm was sounded at 0214.

 Completed action         has/have been + past participle   The beacon has been activated.
  relevant now

 Negative status report     Negative + clear statement        Negative. We are not abandoning ship.

Change active to passive

The officer sounded the alarm at 0214. -> The alarm was sounded at 0214. Keep the time. Add by the officer
when the actor matters. Use were for a plural subject: The valves were closed.

Report the stage accurately

The area has been checked does not mean entry is authorised. Prepared does not mean released, and under
control does not mean extinguished. State only the status confirmed by the responsible person.

Different signals, different purposes

MAYDAY concerns grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. PAN-PAN gives urgency
priority below distress; SECURITE introduces safety information. The message content depends on the
situation. This grammar lesson is not a complete GMDSS or firefighting procedure.

UNIT 7 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

Clear Orders on the Mooring Deck

  Before you read
  Does “I understand” tell the bridge that a line is already fast?

Reading focus: Separate acknowledgement, action in progress and completion.

A Mooring communication needs a named line and a clear action. A message about that rope is difficult
to follow when several lines are moving. The bridge and the station leader must also distinguish an order
from a warning and a report. Each type of message has a different purpose.

B In this tabletop exercise, the bridge orders the forward station to slack away the forward spring. The
station leader first confirms the named action. When the simulated action starts, the leader reports that
the team is slacking away the forward spring. After the action, the leader reports the condition of the line.
An acknowledgement, a progress report and a completion report are not interchangeable.

C A second card introduces a person standing inside a bight. The station leader warns of the danger and
gives a clear instruction to move clear. This is not optional advice. Personnel should never stand in a
bight of rope. A painted area on a deck cannot prove that all other areas are safe: the whole mooring
deck can present danger when lines may come under tension.

D Anchoring uses some related verbs but different equipment. A report that the cable is leading ahead
describes its direction from the hawse pipe; it does not by itself prove that the anchor is holding. Students
use the separate anchor diagram to practise that distinction. All movements in this lesson use paper
counters, not loaded ropes, live winches or operational radios. The ship's procedures govern real
operations.

or curved part of a rope

title: Orders, warnings and status reports
text:
UNIT 7 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Orders, warnings and status reports

Name the station, line or equipment so the receiver knows what the message concerns. Keep an
acknowledgement separate from action in progress and completion. Do not claim that an action has started
before it actually has.

 Function             Form                      Example

 Order                  base verb + named line           Slack away the forward spring.

 Acknowledgement         confirm the received instruction    Slack away the forward spring. Understood.

  Action in progress          am/is/are + verb-ing         We are slacking away the forward spring.

 Completed state            clear status statement           Forward station is all fast.

 Warning             WARNING + hazard          WARNING. The forward spring is under heavy
                                                                          strain.

 Safety prohibition       Do not + base verb           Do not stand in the bight.

There is no universal -ing repeat-back rule

Standard wheel orders are repeated in the same words. Other exchanges require the correct
acknowledgement for their context. A progress report uses -ing only when the action is in progress; a
completion report comes after verification.

Do not weaken a safety instruction

Keeping clear of a bight is not optional advice. State the prohibition or danger clearly. Treat the whole working
mooring deck as a potential danger area; being outside a painted zone does not guarantee safety.

One clear communication route, with urgent warnings allowed

Normally use the agreed station-to-bridge communication arrangement. Any person who sees immediate
danger must be able to raise the alarm or warning under the vessel's procedures. Do not wait to report a
hazard merely because you are not the station leader.

CHIEF OFFICER Loading master, confirm the sequence. Holds two and four first, then one and three.

title: Countable and uncountable quantities
text:
UNIT 8 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Countable nouns and quantifiers

A countable noun names separate items: a container, two pumps. An uncountable noun names a substance
or a general category: fuel, equipment. Use a unit or counting phrase when you need an exact quantity.

 Use                   Countable examples           Uncountable examples

 Nouns                     containers, drums, trucks,           fuel, ballast water, equipment, information
                      pumps

 Question             How many containers?        How much cargo?

 Large quantity          many / a large number of       much / a large amount of cargo
                            containers

 Small positive quantity    a few drums                  a little fuel

 Smaller quantity           fewer trucks                       less ballast water

 Exact quantity             three pumps / twenty tonnes       three items of equipment / twenty tonnes of
                                                          cargo

Count the unit, not the substance

How much cargo remains? How many tonnes remain? Cargo refers to the material collectively; tonnes are
countable units. Include the unit when reporting a number.

Common general meanings

Equipment, machinery and information are uncountable in the meanings used here: two items of equipment,
not two equipments. Cargo usually functions as a mass noun here, although cargoes can mean separate
loads. Damage is uncountable for physical harm; legal damages has a different meaning.

A few / few and a little / little

A few containers means some containers. Few containers emphasises a small number. A little fuel means
some fuel; little fuel emphasises that the amount is small. In positive everyday sentences, a lot of is often more
natural than much.

The Purifier Trips Again

  The situation
  At 0930 LT the Fourth Engineer reports a second trip. Readings and comparison values describe this
  invented system only. The exchange is a reporting model, not authority to open hot fuel equipment.

FOURTH ENGINEER Second Engineer, the fuel-oil purifier has tripped again. The alarm appeared at 0918,
about three hours after the earlier reset at 0620.

SECOND ENGINEER What alarm and readings were recorded?

FOURTH ENGINEER High outlet temperature. The heater outlet reading was 102 degrees Celsius; the
recorded reference for this operation is 98 degrees. Feed-pump suction pressure was 0.8 bar compared with
the earlier 1.2 bar. I have not carried out an internal inspection.

not reset again without authorisation. We need to review the alarm history and the approved procedure.

FOURTH ENGINEER Is a blocked strainer a possible explanation?

opening, authorised personnel must complete the required risk assessment, permits and verified isolation of
every relevant energy source. A tag alone is not proof of safe isolation.

OOW Engine control room, bridge. Does the defect affect manoeuvring?

available clean service-tank fuel is adequate for the present operation. We will report any change immediately
and give the next update by 1200. A repair time is not confirmed.

FOURTH ENGINEER I will record the event time, alarm, readings, action restrictions and next report. I will keep
suspected causes separate from findings.

complete.

title: Report the Symptom, Check the Cause
text:
UNIT 9 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

Report the Symptom, Check the Cause

  Before you read
  Does an alarm message prove the underlying cause of a machinery fault?

Reading focus: Separate readings, possible causes, findings and current status.

A A useful machinery report starts with what has been observed. A low reading, an alarm and unusual
vibration are symptoms. An explanation for them is a possible cause until it is checked. Calling a
component blocked before it has been inspected turns an assumption into a finding and can mislead the
next person.

B At 0918 LT in this fictional training case, fresh-water transfer pump P2 trips. Its discharge pressure
before the trip is 1.6 bar; the comparison reading from the previous stable run was 3.0 bar under the
same stated conditions. The Fourth Engineer reports the readings and time. No leak is visible during the
external check. The engineer does not open any joint or attempt another reset.

C The Second Engineer arranges an authorised investigation under the vessel's procedures. The training
status card must confirm the required isolation, release of stored energy and permission before students
advance the paper exercise. In one version of the task, the isolation record has not been signed. The
group stops at that point, reports the missing authorisation and records that the inspection has not yet
started. A classroom checklist is not a real work permit.

D In the completed case, the authorised inspection finds debris in the suction strainer. That is a finding.
After cleaning and authorised recommissioning at 1105, the discharge pressure is 3.0 bar under the
comparison conditions. The engineer records the result and a further observation time of 1135. The
improvement supports investigation of the restriction, but the reason debris entered the system still needs
review. The final report separates the symptom, the confirmed finding, the action and the present status.
It does not turn a successful restart into proof that every cause has been found.

title: Passive reports; present perfect and past simple
text:
UNIT 9 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Passive reports; present perfect and past simple

Use the present perfect for a past event whose result or unfinished time period matters now. Use the past
simple for an event located in a finished past time. Use a passive form when the affected equipment or
action is the focus.

 Use                 Form                      Example

 General process            is/are + past participle          The fuel is heated before separation.

 Finished past action       was/were + past participle       The strainer was cleaned at 1100 yesterday.

 Event with current result   has/have + past participle        The pump has stopped and is unavailable.

 Passive current result     has/have been + past participle   The unit has been isolated.

 Question about work so   Have/Has + subject + past       What have you checked?
  far                           participle?

 Finished event time        past simple                   The alarm sounded at 0918.

A time expression does not always require past simple

Yesterday and at 0918 in a finished report locate past events. Today, so far and since 0800 can refer to an
unfinished period: The pump has stopped twice today. Use meaning, not the mere presence of a time word.

Already and yet

Already usually goes between have and the participle: I have already checked the reading. Yet commonly
ends a negative or question: I have not checked it yet. Have you checked it yet?

Keep language evidence-based

An alarm or low pressure is an observed symptom. A suspected restriction is a hypothesis. A recorded
inspection finding is evidence. Do not turn an untested explanation into a confirmed cause. Neither a grammar
pattern nor a diagram authorises maintenance.

A Shackle on the Mooring Deck

  The situation
  At 1437 LT the Chief Officer begins collecting accounts of a dropped object. The event time and distances
  are estimates unless stated otherwise.

CHIEF OFFICER Cadet, tell me what you saw and heard. Keep that separate from what you think caused it.

DECK CADET At about 1435 I was by the after bollards. I heard a metallic noise and a shackle landed about
two metres from me. It bounced once and stopped near the hatch coaming.

CHIEF OFFICER Where did it land, and what is known about its weight?

DECK CADET Port side, abreast of the number two crane pedestal. The estimate recorded afterwards was
about six kilograms. Two ratings were about five metres forward of me.

CHIEF OFFICER Bosun, what were you doing before the object fell?

BOSUN I was greasing the jib sheave. I had two shackles in a bag. I had not secured the bag to the structure.
When I moved along the jib, it tipped.

CHIEF OFFICER I will record that as your statement. I cordoned off the area and stopped work aloft at 1437.
Cadet, record that confirmed time.

DECK CADET Nobody was injured. Do we still report it?

CHIEF OFFICER Yes. It is a near-miss. A heavy object falling from the estimated fourteen-metre height could
have caused a serious or fatal head injury. That is a possible outcome, not an injury that occurred.

BOSUN The permit copy does not include a specific check for securing loose gear.

CHIEF OFFICER That is a finding to investigate alongside the work plan, equipment and supervision. It does
not establish a final root cause by itself. I will request a review and hand over the unfinished actions with an
owner and deadline.

title: A Near Miss Is Information Worth Keeping
text:
UNIT 10 | B3 READING FOR MEANING

A Near Miss Is Information Worth Keeping

  Before you read
 Why might an event without injury still need a written report?

Reading focus: Read evidence, preserve uncertainty and hand over follow-up work.

A A near-miss report records an event that could have caused harm but did not. The absence of an injury
does not make the information useless. A useful report helps the next watch understand what happened,
what was done and which questions remain. It should also distinguish something seen directly from
information received from another person.

B In the fictional scene in Visual Resource 10, a tool falls from a raised platform at approximately 1435
LT. It lands about two metres from a cadet. The cadet sees it land but does not see where it was stored
before it fell. Two ratings are nearby. At 1437 the supervisor stops the work and arranges for the area to
be kept clear. Nobody is reported injured.

C The person working on the platform later states that the tool bag was not secured. This is recorded as
that person's statement, not as something the cadet saw. A review of the permit finds no recorded
loose-tool check. This may be a contributing factor, but the report does not declare a final root cause
before the wider investigation. Equipment, planning, supervision and the task conditions may all need
examination.

D The handover identifies two follow-up actions. The Chief Officer is to review the permit wording by 20
September at 1200 LT. The bosun is to check that the barrier remains in place at 1600 LT today. Each
item has an owner and a deadline. When the next officer receives the handover, the officer confirms both
actions and asks about any uncertainty. Times described as approximate remain approximate in the
written account. A complete record preserves the evidence instead of making it seem more certain than it
really is.

witness statement: an account from a person who saw or heard the event   |  contributing factor: something that may
help explain an event   |  follow-up: later work to check or complete an action

title: Past tenses and reported speech
text:
UNIT 10 | C GRAMMAR - FORMS AND MEANING

Past tenses and reported speech

An incident account distinguishes an activity in progress, a completed event and an earlier event. Reported
speech identifies whose account is being recorded. Keep the wording neutral and preserve any uncertainty
in the source statement.

 Meaning             Form                      Example

 Background action        was/were + verb-ing            The bosun was greasing the sheave when the
                                                    bag tipped.

 Completed event          past simple                A shackle landed near the cadet.

  Earlier past event        had + past participle           He had not secured the bag before he moved.

  Attributed statement        said/stated/reported + that       The bosun stated that he had not secured the
                           clause                          bag.

 Passive action           was/were + past participle       The area was cordoned off at 1437.

 Uncertain detail           about / approximately / not       The witness estimated the time as about 1435.
                           recorded

When and while connect events

I was checking the deck when the tool fell: an action in progress and an interrupting event. While often
introduces a continuing background action, but the conjunction alone does not mechanically determine the
tense.

Backshift where the reporting context requires it

Direct: “I did not secure the bag.” Reported: The worker said that the bag had not been secured. Change
pronouns and time references carefully. Backshift is common in past accounts, but not compulsory when the
original statement remains true and the context supports retaining its tense.

Do not invent evidence to replace blame

The worker was careless is an evaluation, not a description of what was seen. Replace it only with an
observation or an attributed statement actually supplied. A blank checklist is a finding; it does not, by itself,
establish every underlying cause.

  You are on MV LARCH, call sign HSTQ4, in a CLOSED classroom simulator. Call Harbour Control.

  Your role and information
  You are an engine cadet reporting to the Second Engineer. Fresh-water pump P5 stopped at 1420 LT
  with a motor overload alarm. A recorded pressure just before the trip was 2.5 bar. P1 is now running and
  the water supply is maintained. No internal inspection or reset has been carried out. Cause not
  confirmed. The next update is required at 1500 LT. Give a short report and answer the examiner's
  questions. Deck cadets practise the same shared operational reporting task.

Prepare for two minutes; speak for up to four minutes. The examiner will ask questions. Ask for clarification
when you need it.
